topics.name: Nested loops in code
topics.description: Write, run, read and alter code (block-based or text-based) that places one loop inside another (for example a loop that draws a square, repeated with a turn after each square to make a rotating pattern), predict how many times the inner steps run altogether (outer repeats × inner repeats), and describe how changing the inner or the outer loop changes the outcome
topics.originalDescription: Write, run, read and alter code (block-based or text-based) that places one loop inside another (for example a loop that draws a square, repeated with a turn after each square to make a rotating pattern), predict how many times the inner steps run altogether (outer repeats × inner repeats), and describe how changing the inner or the outer loop changes the outcome
topics.subject: computacao
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.

prerequisites.reason: testing and debugging supports checking the predicted repeat count
a nested loop is a loop whose body contains a loop: writing, predicting and altering it needs the single-loop procedure
a decision placed inside a loop is an allowed alternative nested structure (glossary example), not required
following repetition with steps inside it in a flowchart supports reasoning about nested structure

evidence: Write and run code with a loop inside a loop (e.g. repeat a 'draw a square' loop 6 times with a turn after each square) and check that the result matches the plan
Read a program with nested loops and predict how many times the inner action happens altogether (e.g. repeat 3 [repeat 4 [clap]] claps 12 times), then run it to check
Change either the inner or the outer repeat count in nested-loop code, then explain and test how the change affects what happens

topics.name: Gerunds as nouns
topics.description: Recognise a gerund - an -ing form of a verb that works as a noun to name an activity - whether it is the subject ("Swimming keeps me fit"), the object ("I enjoy swimming") or comes after a preposition ("She is good at swimming"); tell it apart from an -ing verb in a progressive tense ("She is swimming") and from an -ing word describing a noun ("the swimming dog"); and use this to understand and write sentences clearly.

topics.name: Blending spoken sounds
topics.description: Listen to a word spoken as separate speech sounds (phonemes) - with no printed word, letters, letter names or answer pictures - and combine them to say the whole word, from two sounds (“sh-e” → “she”) to longer sequences, including consonant clusters at the start or end (“f-r-o-g” → “frog”, “j-u-m-p” → “jump”). An adult says each sound clearly with brief, natural pauses and without adding “uh”; the child says the word naturally in their own accent. The examples show the kind of words used; they are not levels, a list or a limit.

evidence: Use the root-word clue for endings that sound like /ʃəs/: when the root word ends in -ce, the ending is usually -cious (space → spacious, grace → gracious, vice → vicious, malice → malicious); learn other -cious and -tious words (such as precious, cautious and ambitious) as words to know, noting exceptions such as anxious
Choose between -cial (usually after a vowel: special, official) and -tial (usually after a consonant: essential, partial) when spelling words with the /ʃəl/ ending

Choose -ant/-ance/-ancy or -ent/-ence/-ency using clues: -ent/-ence/-ency after a soft c, soft g or qu sound (innocent/innocence, intelligent, frequent/frequency); -ant/-ance/-ancy when a related word has a clear /æ/ or /eɪ/ sound, often an -ation word (observation → observant/observance, hesitation → hesitant/hesitancy); -ent/-ence when a related word has a clear /ɛ/ sound (confidential → confident/confidence); a hard c or g sound heard just before the ending can be a possible clue for -ant (significant, elegant); and learn the many words where no clue decides

standards.description: develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems

plan and conduct statistical investigations by posing and refining questions or identifying a problem and collecting relevant data; analyse and interpret the data and communicate findings within the context of the investigation

Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data related to the question and accounts for it in the answers. For example, "How old am I?" is not a statistical question, but "How old are the students in my school?" is a statistical question because one anticipates variability in students' ages.

prerequisites.reason: Experience asking and answering questions about collected categorical data gives the concrete basis for recognising which questions need data that varies
Terms such as data, sample and average help pupils describe the population, attribute and expected variation

evidence: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data - even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')

topics.name: How far apart two groups are
topics.originalName: How far apart two groups are
topics.description: Compare two numerical distributions with similar variability shown on a shared scale (e.g. dot plots) in two distinct ways: (1) judge their actual visual overlap directly from the displays - how much of each group's data lies among the other group's values; and (2) separately, find the difference between their centres and express it as a multiple of a clearly named measure of variability of either group, using matching measures (difference in means ÷ MAD, or difference in medians ÷ IQR), interpreting a larger multiple as centres that are further apart relative to the typical spread. Recognise that the same difference in centres means more when the variability is small, and that for similarly shaped, roughly symmetric, single-peaked distributions a larger multiple usually goes with less overlap - but that the ratio alone does not determine overlap: skew, clusters, gaps or outliers can make the visible overlap greater or smaller than the ratio suggests, so overlap is always checked on the display; and this simple ratio is only appropriate when the two variabilities are similar

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. standards.description: estimate, construct and measure angles in degrees, using appropriate tools including a protractor, and relate these measures to angle names

An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and-if there is a flaw in an argument-explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y - 2)/(x - 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x - 1)(x + 1), (x - 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x - 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

The +1 pattern in counting is the earliest repeated reasoning

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, “Does this make sense?” They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize-to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents-and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 - 3(x - y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y - 2)/(x - 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x - 1)(x + 1), (x - 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x - 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, “Does this make sense?” They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 - 3(x - y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and-if there is a flaw in an argument-explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. standards.description: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize-to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents-and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and-if there is a flaw in an argument-explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, “Does this make sense?” They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y - 2)/(x - 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x - 1)(x + 1), (x - 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x - 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 - 3(x - y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and-if there is a flaw in an argument-explain what it is. standards.description: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, “Does this make sense?” They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

standards.description: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize-to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents-and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two-column table. For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), ...
Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.
Use ratio reasoning to convert measurement units; manipulate and transform units appropriately when multiplying or dividing quantities.
change freely between related standard units [for example time, length, area, volume/capacity, mass]
Convert between different units of measure [for example, kilometre to metre; hour to minute]
solve problems involving converting from hours to minutes; minutes to seconds; years to months; weeks to days
Convert between different units of metric measure (for example, kilometre and metre; centimetre and metre; centimetre and millimetre; gram and kilogram; litre and millilitre).
Solve problems involving converting between units of time.

Use, read, write and convert between standard units, converting measurements of length, mass, volume and time from a smaller unit of measure to a larger unit, and vice versa, using decimal notation to up to three decimal places.

prerequisites.reason: Decimal powers-of-ten arithmetic supports decimal metric examples, not every unit-conversion task; it is not a universal grade-based gate.
generic unit conversion (equivalent amount via the unit factor) does not require standard mass/capacity arithmetic
generic conversion does not require whole calendar facts (days in each month, leap years); time examples are optional families
Iterating length units can illustrate relative unit size, but practical length measurement is not required for time or other unit conversions.
A conversion factor expresses equal groups of smaller units within one larger unit; multiplicative unit reasoning is essential.
Multiplication and division by powers of ten support metric conversions; non-base-ten time rates use their actual relationships.

evidence: Convert 3.25 kg to 3250 g and 45 cm to 0.45 m, explaining why the count grows or shrinks; convert 5 g to 0.005 kg without adding or deleting zeros mechanically

Convert 8 weeks 3 days to 59 days and 2 years 3 months to 27 months; explain why an unspecified month cannot be converted to one fixed number of days
Build and interpret a two-column equivalence table for cm and mm, explain the factor, and use the same relationship to convert in either direction
Convert 2.5 hours to 9000 seconds through minutes, tracking the unit at each step and checking by reversing the conversion

standards.description: Understand the concept of a unit rate a/b associated with a ratio a:b with b ≠ 0, and use rate language in the context of a ratio relationship. For example, "This recipe has a ratio of 3 cups of flour to 4 cups of sugar, so there is 3/4 cup of flour for each cup of sugar." "We paid $75 for 15 hamburgers, which is a rate of $5 per hamburger."

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

topics.name: Types of Metamorphosis
topics.description: Complete vs incomplete metamorphosis. Complete: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterflies, beetles, flies). Incomplete: egg → nymph → adult - the nymph looks like a small version of the adult and moults as it grows (grasshoppers, dragonflies, crickets). Why do some insects transform completely while others grow gradually?

topics.name: Indigenous cultural renewal in Canada
topics.description: Explain in age-appropriate terms how colonial policies in Canada, including residential schooling, disrupted many First Nations, Métis and Inuit family, language and cultural connections. Use attributed contemporary community-led examples to explain cultural renewal and its relationship to identity and belonging, while recognizing distinct peoples and continuing cultures.
topics.originalDescription: Explain in age-appropriate terms how colonial policies in Canada, including residential schooling, disrupted many First Nations, Métis and Inuit family, language and cultural connections. Use attributed contemporary community-led examples to explain cultural renewal and its relationship to identity and belonging, while recognizing distinct peoples and continuing cultures.
topics.subject: historia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Explain that colonial policies, including residential schools, separated many Indigenous children from their families and suppressed languages and cultural practices; do not imply that every person had the same experience or that cultures disappeared.
Using a named community-authoritative account, identify who leads a contemporary cultural or language renewal initiative and what is being strengthened or reclaimed.
Explain how the example can reconnect people with family, community knowledge or cultural identity, rather than merely say that the project is nice or respectful.
Transfer the historical-disruption, community-action and identity relationship to another attributed example, keeping its people and source distinct.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After hearing an attributed, age-appropriate account of a community-led renewal project, can {{name}} explain who leads it, what is being strengthened, and how it connects people with culture and belonging after colonial disruption, including residential schooling? Can they explain a second example without treating all First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples as one culture?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After hearing an attributed, age-appropriate account of a community-led renewal project, can {{name}} explain who leads it, what is being strengthened, and how it connects people with culture and belonging after colonial disruption, including residential schooling? Can they explain a second example without treating all First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples as one culture?

topics.name: Traditional and treaty territories in Canada
topics.originalName: Traditional and treaty territories in Canada
topics.description: Use attributed, locally verified resources to identify the traditional Indigenous territory or territories and applicable treaty reference for a Canadian place. Distinguish traditional territory, a treaty area or relationship, and a present-day reserve; these references are not interchangeable and may involve more than one people or account.
topics.originalDescription: Use attributed, locally verified resources to identify the traditional Indigenous territory or territories and applicable treaty reference for a Canadian place. Distinguish traditional territory, a treaty area or relationship, and a present-day reserve; these references are not interchangeable and may involve more than one people or account.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Name the peoples and traditional territory or territories identified for a place by the supplied locally verified sources, attributing each account rather than assuming one exclusive owner.
Identify the applicable treaty by its full name or number and regional context when the sources establish one; do not invent a treaty where the verified resources do not establish one.

Explain that traditional territory concerns a people’s enduring connections with lands and waters, a treaty records a particular agreement or relationship, and a present reserve is a particular designated land area rather than the whole traditional territory.

Use a second verified place/resource packet to identify its different territorial and treaty references; explain why the nearest reserve or a municipal boundary alone cannot establish those references.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With an adult-prepared, attributed publicly available, locally verified resource packet for a school, can {{name}} name the traditional territory or territories and the applicable treaty reference that the sources support? Can they explain why the traditional territory, treaty reference and present reserve are different, then use a second place’s packet without carrying over the first place’s names or treating the nearest reserve as the answer?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: With an adult-prepared, attributed publicly available, locally verified resource packet for a school, can {{name}} name the traditional territory or territories and the applicable treaty reference that the sources support? Can they explain why the traditional territory, treaty reference and present reserve are different, then use a second place’s packet without carrying over the first place’s names or treating the nearest reserve as the answer?

topics.name: Matching a sounded pitch
topics.description: Listen to a comfortable reference pitch and intentionally reproduce it with the voice or a suitable pitched instrument, comparing the result with the reference and adjusting higher or lower when needed. Repeat the matching with a new reference. This is relative matching to a heard model, not naming an absolute note or explaining vibration physics.
topics.originalDescription: Listen to a comfortable reference pitch and intentionally reproduce it with the voice or a suitable pitched instrument, comparing the result with the reference and adjusting higher or lower when needed. Repeat the matching with a new reference. This is relative matching to a heard model, not naming an absolute note or explaining vibration physics.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Reproduce a comfortable reference pitch after hearing it, rather than only label it high or low or change loudness.
Listen to a comparison between the reference and their attempt and adjust the produced pitch towards the reference; showing the adjustment is sufficient without technical language.
Match a different comfortable reference using the voice or a suitable pitched instrument, without relying on a fixed remembered note.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After you sound a comfortable note, can {{name}} copy its pitch by humming, singing or using a suitable pitched instrument, listen again and adjust if needed? Can they do it with a different note too?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After you sound a comfortable note, can {{name}} copy its pitch by humming, singing or using a suitable pitched instrument, listen again and adjust if needed? Can they do it with a different note too?

topics.name: Creating and shaping musical sound
topics.description: Create or improvise a short piece of musical sound for an intended idea or situation. Choose and organise sounds and silences, listen to the result and deliberately adjust timing, sound quality, loudness or a musical contrast to shape the intended audible effect. Present and adapt the result. Voice, body, suitable instruments or found sounds may be used; a repeating mathematical rule, pitched singing and written notation are not required.
topics.originalDescription: Create or improvise a short piece of musical sound for an intended idea or situation. Choose and organise sounds and silences, listen to the result and deliberately adjust timing, sound quality, loudness or a musical contrast to shape the intended audible effect. Present and adapt the result. Voice, body, suitable instruments or found sounds may be used; a repeating mathematical rule, pitched singing and written notation are not required.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Create an own short musical sound piece with deliberate sound and silence choices, rather than only copy a model or explain an abstract sequence rule.
Listen to two versions or an attempt and adjust an audible musical feature such as a phrase contrast, timing, loudness, sound quality or ending for an intended effect.
Present the chosen sound piece and adapt it for another idea, situation or available sound source, demonstrating the intended audible difference.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} invent a short musical sound piece, listen to it and change a sound, silence or timing choice to make the effect they intend? Can they let you hear that choice and adapt the piece for a new idea?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} invent a short musical sound piece, listen to it and change a sound, silence or timing choice to make the effect they intend? Can they let you hear that choice and adapt the piece for a new idea?

topics.name: Creating and performing expressive movement sequences
topics.originalName: Creating and performing expressive movement sequences
topics.description: Choose, combine and practise a short sequence of body movements to express an everyday action, idea or experience, using movement qualities or spatial choices intentionally. Perform the chosen sequence and vary or adapt it for a different intention or situation. Movement may be seated or standing within safe available access; no fixed dance style, athletic norm, costume or spoken script is required.
topics.originalDescription: Choose, combine and practise a short sequence of body movements to express an everyday action, idea or experience, using movement qualities or spatial choices intentionally. Perform the chosen sequence and vary or adapt it for a different intention or situation. Movement may be seated or standing within safe available access; no fixed dance style, athletic norm, costume or spoken script is required.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Create and practise a recognisable ordered sequence of own movement choices, rather than only copy isolated teacher actions.
Use a purposeful contrast in movement quality, direction, level, shape or use of space to support the intended action or idea.
Perform the chosen sequence with its intended order and adapt it for a new intention or situation, showing the changed choices.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} make, practise and perform a short movement sequence to show an idea or everyday action, then change how they move to show a different intention? They may explain by demonstrating or pointing; a spoken script is not required.
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} make, practise and perform a short movement sequence to show an idea or everyday action, then change how they move to show a different intention? They may explain by demonstrating or pointing; a spoken script is not required.

topics.name: Composing visual artwork
topics.description: Choose and organise visual elements and suitable materials in an artwork to express an observation, idea, experience or feeling. Try an arrangement, make a purposeful change and present the intended effect through the work, demonstration, pointing or ordinary language. The operation is visual organisation and expression rather than accurate lettering, a prescribed realistic picture, selling a product or producing a functional design solution.
topics.originalDescription: Choose and organise visual elements and suitable materials in an artwork to express an observation, idea, experience or feeling. Try an arrangement, make a purposeful change and present the intended effect through the work, demonstration, pointing or ordinary language. The operation is visual organisation and expression rather than accurate lettering, a prescribed realistic picture, selling a product or producing a functional design solution.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Make own choices about the arrangement of visual elements such as line, form, colour, space or texture for an intended visual effect or meaning.
Compare or try an alternative arrangement and make a purposeful change rather than only reproduce an adult’s finished model.
Compose a further work or adapt a composition for a different intention, material or available space, indicating how the changed choices support the effect.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With suitable art materials, can {{name}} choose how to arrange the visual elements for their own idea, try a change and show what difference it makes? Can they adapt the composition when the idea, materials or space changes?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: With suitable art materials, can {{name}} choose how to arrange the visual elements for their own idea, try a change and show what difference it makes? Can they adapt the composition when the idea, materials or space changes?

topics.name: Sound and noise in context
topics.description: Understand noise in everyday listening contexts as sound that is unwanted or interferes with an activity. Explain that a sound may be useful or welcome in one situation and noise for a particular listener or purpose in another, while remaining sound in both. A noise judgment is not determined just by loudness, source or whether it is musical.
topics.originalDescription: Understand noise in everyday listening contexts as sound that is unwanted or interferes with an activity. Explain that a sound may be useful or welcome in one situation and noise for a particular listener or purpose in another, while remaining sound in both. A noise judgment is not determined just by loudness, source or whether it is musical.
topics.subject: ciencias
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify an unwanted or interfering sound in a supplied everyday situation and give a context-relevant reason; recognise that it remains a sound.
Compare the same comfortable sound in two situations or for two listeners and explain why it can be useful or wanted in one and noise in the other.
Apply the distinction to a new situation without assuming that all music is welcome, all machine sounds are noise or every loud sound is unwanted.
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the same short bell sound helps people know when to change activity but keeps interrupting a quiet conversation, can {{name}} explain why it might be wanted in one situation and noise in the other, and that it is a sound in both?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: If the same short bell sound helps people know when to change activity but keeps interrupting a quiet conversation, can {{name}} explain why it might be wanted in one situation and noise in the other, and that it is a sound in both?

topics.name: Mémoriser et réemployer le vocabulaire
topics.description: Understand the French word forms and meanings in taught familiar-topic vocabulary sets, retain them beyond immediate repetition, and independently use them appropriately in French conversation or play.
topics.originalDescription: Understand the French word forms and meanings in taught familiar-topic vocabulary sets, retain them beyond immediate repetition, and independently use them appropriately in French conversation or play.
topics.subject: frances
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify the meaning of taught French nouns, actions and feeling words in a familiar spoken message or scene, rather than infer success from English vocabulary.
Retrieve the French word forms after a delay and use them appropriately without an immediate spoken model.
Use taught French vocabulary independently in a different familiar scene or exchange, showing meaning as well as a memorized sound sequence.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} learns a small set of French words for objects, actions and feelings, can they identify their meanings in a new French message, then a few days later independently use the French words appropriately in another familiar scene or conversation rather than only echoing a model?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After {{name}} learns a small set of French words for objects, actions and feelings, can they identify their meanings in a new French message, then a few days later independently use the French words appropriately in another familiar scene or conversation rather than only echoing a model?

topics.name: Articuler les consonnes
topics.description: Produce intelligible French consonant contrasts, including t/k, f/v, s/z, p/b, t/d, k/g and ch compared with s/j/z, and retain consonants in clusters such as br, cr, bl and pl in words and short phrases. Judge meaningful contrasts using a qualified model of the intended French variety, without treating a legitimate accent difference as an error.
topics.originalDescription: Produce intelligible French consonant contrasts, including t/k, f/v, s/z, p/b, t/d, k/g and ch compared with s/j/z, and retain consonants in clusters such as br, cr, bl and pl in words and short phrases. Judge meaningful contrasts using a qualified model of the intended French variety, without treating a legitimate accent difference as an error.
topics.subject: frances
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Produce French words that preserve the intended t/k, f/v, s/z, p/b, t/d and k/g contrasts, using familiar meaningful examples.
Keep French ch distinct from s, j and z where those are distinct in the target variety; make the intended word intelligible in a phrase.
Produce br, cr, bl and pl clusters without dropping a consonant, and transfer the operation to another familiar word rather than only echo a practiced list.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Using familiar French words and a qualified French model, can {{name}} say contrasting words such as poule/boule and chou/sou distinctly and keep the consonants in bras, crabe, bleu and pluie? Can a listener distinguish the intended words in a short phrase and in another familiar word carrying the same contrast, without relying only on immediate repetition?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Using familiar French words and a qualified French model, can {{name}} say contrasting words such as poule/boule and chou/sou distinctly and keep the consonants in bras, crabe, bleu and pluie? Can a listener distinguish the intended words in a short phrase and in another familiar word carrying the same contrast, without relying only on immediate repetition?

topics.name: Distinguer les voyelles nasales
topics.description: Hear and produce the French oral/nasal vowel distinctions and contrasts among nasal vowels used in the intended French variety. Use meaningful familiar words and respect regional phonetic variation, including whether the in/un contrast is maintained; do not assume that every French variety has only three nasal vowels.
topics.originalDescription: Hear and produce the French oral/nasal vowel distinctions and contrasts among nasal vowels used in the intended French variety. Use meaningful familiar words and respect regional phonetic variation, including whether the in/un contrast is maintained; do not assume that every French variety has only three nasal vowels.
topics.subject: frances
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify which familiar word a speaker says in oral/nasal contrast examples, using meaning or pictures so a spoken French answer is not required to demonstrate listening.
Produce familiar words with oral versus nasal vowels intelligibly and preserve the nasal-vowel contrasts of the target variety, including in/un where distinct.
Recognize and produce the same contrasts in another voice or familiar word/phrase without merely copying the immediately preceding model.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With familiar French words and a qualified model of the intended variety, can {{name}} hear which word is said in contrasts such as bas/banc, beau/bon and paix/pain, then produce the words distinctly in a short phrase? Include brun/brin when the target variety distinguishes un/in, and check transfer with another voice or familiar word rather than marking a legitimate regional merger wrong.
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: With familiar French words and a qualified model of the intended variety, can {{name}} hear which word is said in contrasts such as bas/banc, beau/bon and paix/pain, then produce the words distinctly in a short phrase? Include brun/brin when the target variety distinguishes un/in, and check transfer with another voice or familiar word rather than marking a legitimate regional merger wrong.

topics.name: Écrire de mémoire les mots français familiers
topics.originalName: Écrire de mémoire les mots français familiers
topics.description: Know and retain the written forms of taught familiar French words, including appropriate accents and common non-transparent spellings, and independently retrieve those forms in meaningful French writing without copying a written model.
topics.originalDescription: Know and retain the written forms of taught familiar French words, including appropriate accents and common non-transparent spellings, and independently retrieve those forms in meaningful French writing without copying a written model.
topics.subject: frances
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Write taught familiar French words correctly after a delay without a visible written model, preserving their letters and accents.
Retrieve taught French spellings not fully predictable from the spoken form, such as monsieur, femme or temps, in a phrase or meaning context that disambiguates the intended word.
Independently reuse the taught written French forms correctly in a changed meaningful message, rather than only copy, recognise a printed choice or supply the English spelling.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After {{name}} has learned some familiar French words, can they write them correctly a few days later, including accents and spellings such as monsieur or beaucoup, then use them correctly in a new short French message without copying a model?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After {{name}} has learned some familiar French words, can they write them correctly a few days later, including accents and spellings such as monsieur or beaucoup, then use them correctly in a new short French message without copying a model?

topics.name: French-speaking communities in Ontario
topics.description: Identify distinct French-speaking communities in Ontario and explain, through attributed contemporary examples, how their cultural activities and creative work contribute to French-language life. Use the Ottawa and Sudbury cases to connect a place, an actual cultural activity or creator and its contribution, while recognising that a city and its French-speaking communities contain varied people and practices.
topics.originalDescription: Identify distinct French-speaking communities in Ontario and explain, through attributed contemporary examples, how their cultural activities and creative work contribute to French-language life. Use the Ottawa and Sudbury cases to connect a place, an actual cultural activity or creator and its contribution, while recognising that a city and its French-speaking communities contain varied people and practices.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify Ottawa and Sudbury as Ontario places with French-speaking communities; distinguish them from a supplied example outside Ontario without assuming every resident speaks French.

Explain the attributed Ottawa festival, Ottawa-connected children’s author and Sudbury theatre examples, connecting their actual activities or works with French-language creation, sharing or cultural exchange.

Use another supplied attributed community example to explain a supported similarity or difference and what it adds to the account, without treating one event, language or creator as every person’s culture.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After learning about French-language cultural life in Ottawa and Sudbury, can {{name}} name the places and explain how the studied festival, children’s author and theatre contribute? With another community’s short account, can they make a supported comparison without assuming everybody in either place has the same culture?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After learning about French-language cultural life in Ottawa and Sudbury, can {{name}} name the places and explain how the studied festival, children’s author and theatre contribute? With another community’s short account, can they make a supported comparison without assuming everybody in either place has the same culture?

topics.name: French-speaking communities in Quebec
topics.description: Know a bounded contemporary repertoire of French-speaking community life in Quebec through Montréal and Québec City, with the Baie-Saint-Paul origins of one studied creative organisation. Connect the book salon, museum and circus-creation examples to their actual places, cultural activities and supported contributions, while distinguishing a city or language from everybody’s identity and practices.
topics.originalDescription: Know a bounded contemporary repertoire of French-speaking community life in Quebec through Montréal and Québec City, with the Baie-Saint-Paul origins of one studied creative organisation. Connect the book salon, museum and circus-creation examples to their actual places, cultural activities and supported contributions, while distinguishing a city or language from everybody’s identity and practices.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, identify the named community places and their broad Quebec setting without copying a complete answer list. Distinguish the stated local communities from every resident of a city or region.

Explain all three attributed cultural-activity cases, connecting their actual institution or creative work, location and contribution. Keep origin, current base, institutional mission and a documented activity distinct.

Compare another supplied attributed account with the learned cases using a supported similarity or difference, and state a limit rather than infer everybody’s ancestry, language proficiency, feelings or customs.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After studying French-speaking community life in Quebec, can {{name}} connect Montréal’s book salon, Québec City’s museum and the circus’s Baie-Saint-Paul origins and Montréal creation base with what they contribute? Compare another supplied community account without assuming everyone shares one practice.
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After studying French-speaking community life in Quebec, can {{name}} connect Montréal’s book salon, Québec City’s museum and the circus’s Baie-Saint-Paul origins and Montréal creation base with what they contribute? Compare another supplied community account without assuming everyone shares one practice.

topics.name: French-speaking communities in eastern, western and northern Canada
topics.originalName: French-speaking communities in eastern, western and northern Canada

Locate the studied Moncton, Saint-Boniface and Whitehorse cases broadly, connect their film, festival and community-exhibition activities with supported contributions, and compare the cases without assigning one uniform identity or culture to a city, region or language.

Explain all three attributed cultural-activity cases, connecting their actual institution or creative work, location and contribution. Keep origin, current base, institutional mission and a documented activity distinct.

Compare another supplied attributed account with the learned cases using a supported similarity or difference, and state a limit rather than infer everybody’s ancestry, language proficiency, feelings or customs.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After studying French-speaking community life in eastern, western and northern Canada, can {{name}} identify the Moncton, Saint-Boniface and Whitehorse cases and explain what their cinema, festival and community exhibitions contribute? Use a new supplied account for a supported comparison without assuming everyone lives alike.
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After studying French-speaking community life in eastern, western and northern Canada, can {{name}} identify the Moncton, Saint-Boniface and Whitehorse cases and explain what their cinema, festival and community exhibitions contribute? topics.name: Land use and human needs
topics.description: Distinguish common purposes for which people use land and water, including housing, food production, making and exchanging goods or services, transport, recreation and conservation, and explain how those uses address human needs and wants. Recognize mixed uses and that buildings, vegetation or a natural/managed/built label alone do not establish a place’s purpose; unbuilt places can have important uses.
topics.originalDescription: Distinguish common purposes for which people use land and water, including housing, food production, making and exchanging goods or services, transport, recreation and conservation, and explain how those uses address human needs and wants. Recognize mixed uses and that buildings, vegetation or a natural/managed/built label alone do not establish a place’s purpose; unbuilt places can have important uses.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Use supplied accurate local or regional accounts to distinguish the purpose of places used for homes, food production, making goods, shops/services, transport, recreation and conservation; explain the needs or wants addressed.
Explain a supplied land or water use, including a use without buildings, without treating an unbuilt place as unused or assuming its purpose from appearance alone.
Compare similar-looking places with different stated uses and explain more than one use in a supplied mixed-use example; distinguish the purpose from whether a feature is natural, managed or built.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give {{name}} short, accurate descriptions of places used for homes, growing food, making goods, shops or services, transport, recreation and conservation, including a lake used for fishing. Can they explain what each place is used for and the need or want it helps meet? Then compare homes and a factory, which are both built, and two wooded areas with different stated uses. Try a shop with homes above it: can they explain its two uses, without deciding that a place with no buildings has no use?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Give {{name}} short, accurate descriptions of places used for homes, growing food, making goods, shops or services, transport, recreation and conservation, including a lake used for fishing. Can they explain what each place is used for and the need or want it helps meet? Then compare homes and a factory, which are both built, and two wooded areas with different stated uses. Try a shop with homes above it: can they explain its two uses, without deciding that a place with no buildings has no use?

topics.name: Ontario’s major landform regions
topics.description: Identify the broad Ontario locations and distinguishing landscape characteristics of the Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands using the stated current physical-region convention. Distinguish these physical regions from provincial or community boundaries, and recognize that each broad region includes local variation.
topics.originalDescription: Identify the broad Ontario locations and distinguishing landscape characteristics of the Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands using the stated current physical-region convention. Distinguish these physical regions from provincial or community boundaries, and recognize that each broad region includes local variation.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Name and indicate the broad Ontario locations of the Canadian Shield, Hudson Bay Lowland and Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Lowlands on an outline/reference map.

Describe distinguishing characteristics: the Shield’s widespread rock, rounded terrain and many lakes; the Hudson Bay Lowland’s low-relief wetland plain near Hudson and James bays; and the southern Great Lakes-St. Lawrence plain-like lowlands with local hills and an escarpment.

Recognize the same regional pattern on a differently styled map and explain why physical-region boundaries are not simply province or community boundaries; do not treat a broad region as completely uniform.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After exploring the current physical-region map together with an Ontario outline, show {{name}} an Ontario outline with major waters but without the three region names. Can they name the three broad physical regions from the convention you studied, show their broad locations and explain a characteristic that distinguishes each? Ask whether every location within one region must look identical, and have them explain using a checked Ontario example. Then use a differently styled reference map: can they recognize the same regions without relying on one colour scheme or confusing them with province or community boundaries?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After exploring the current physical-region map together with an Ontario outline, show {{name}} an Ontario outline with major waters but without the three region names. Can they name the three broad physical regions from the convention you studied, show their broad locations and explain a characteristic that distinguishes each? Ask whether every location within one region must look identical, and have them explain using a checked Ontario example. Then use a differently styled reference map: can they recognize the same regions without relying on one colour scheme or confusing them with province or community boundaries?

topics.name: Ontario communities and local governance
topics.description: Distinguish Ontario municipal community types and groupings from First Nations communities and Métis community/region governance, and explain how the governing bodies in verified examples provide services or make development decisions responding to the needs of the people they represent. A community name or geographic boundary alone does not establish its governing authority.
topics.originalDescription: Distinguish Ontario municipal community types and groupings from First Nations communities and Métis community/region governance, and explain how the governing bodies in verified examples provide services or make development decisions responding to the needs of the people they represent. A community name or geographic boundary alone does not establish its governing authority.
topics.subject: desenvolvimento-pessoal-social
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify named, verified Ontario examples of city, town, township, village and county municipal entities; distinguish those from a particular First Nation and a Métis community or regional representative body. Explain that these are not interchangeable municipal tiers.

Using studied verified municipal, First Nation and Métis community/regional examples, identify the relevant governing body and explain a supported service or development relationship. Distinguish a council decision, departmental implementation and Métis representation/consultation rather than assigning identical powers to every council.

Explain from verified contrasting examples why a label such as city or county, physical proximity or a map polygon does not by itself establish who governs whom. Apply this distinction to a fresh verified Ontario example and identify what authority information is needed.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After studying accurate examples, can {{name}} explain how Ontario cities, towns, townships, villages and counties differ from a First Nation and a Métis community or region? Using studied municipal, First Nation and Métis examples, ask who represents the community and how a particular service or development decision meets local needs. Would a nearby city automatically make decisions for the First Nation, or would a Métis council automatically decide city zoning? Try a fresh example: what information would they check before assigning a governing body?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: After studying accurate examples, can {{name}} explain how Ontario cities, towns, townships, villages and counties differ from a First Nation and a Métis community or region? Using studied municipal, First Nation and Métis examples, ask who represents the community and how a particular service or development decision meets local needs. Would a nearby city automatically make decisions for the First Nation, or would a Métis council automatically decide city zoning? Try a fresh example: what information would they check before assigning a governing body?

topics.name: Canadian treaty agreements and historical effects
topics.originalName: Canadian treaty agreements and historical effects
topics.description: Identify a few studied regional agreements involving Indigenous peoples around1780-1850, explain particular parties, commitments and historical effects on communities, and relate an accurately attributed wampum record or continuing agreement relationship to its own purpose and chronology. Distinguish the agreements rather than assuming identical terms or that a present reserve boundary establishes their meaning.
topics.originalDescription: Identify a few studied regional agreements involving Indigenous peoples around1780-1850, explain particular parties, commitments and historical effects on communities, and relate an accurately attributed wampum record or continuing agreement relationship to its own purpose and chronology. Distinguish the agreements rather than assuming identical terms or that a present reserve boundary establishes their meaning.
topics.subject: historia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After studying a verified regional case set, identify selected agreements and their parties and period; explain a specific supported commitment and effect for the communities involved.

Compare agreements with different purposes or terms and distinguish an agreement’s promises from documented subsequent events. Explain an attributed wampum record/relationship without treating it merely as decoration, money or a belt necessarily exchanged for every land agreement.

Keep an earlier continuing wampum relationship chronologically distinct from1780-1850 agreements. Apply the distinction to a further verified agreement/record, using its own source rather than importing the first case’s terms or adjudicating current rights.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After studying a few regional agreements, can {{name}} identify who made them, what a particular agreement promised and how it affected the communities? Compare two with different purposes or terms. Using an attributed account of a wampum belt or relationship, can they explain what it records and when it began, without assuming every agreement had the same terms or every belt was exchanged at the date of a later land agreement?

topics.name: Community life in Canada,1780-1850
topics.description: Know a bounded repertoire of specific First Nations, Métis, Inuit and settler community cases in what is now Canada around1780-1850: locate them broadly in their period, describe documented shelter, food, work and family learning/contributions, and explain supported connections between those ways of life and the local setting. Preserve differences between communities and distinguish dated historical evidence from assumptions about all people today.
topics.originalDescription: Know a bounded repertoire of specific First Nations, Métis, Inuit and settler community cases in what is now Canada around1780-1850: locate them broadly in their period, describe documented shelter, food, work and family learning/contributions, and explain supported connections between those ways of life and the local setting. Preserve differences between communities and distinguish dated historical evidence from assumptions about all people today.

topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, identify and broadly locate distinct First Nation, Métis and Inuit cases and more than one settler community, keeping their periods and identities separate rather than treating all Indigenous people or all settlers as one way of life.

Describe supported aspects of ordinary life across the studied cases, including food/shelter/work and documented contributions of men, women and children. Explain a particular connection to local land/water, materials or community relationships using actual case facts.

Compare two studied cases with a supported similarity and difference, then interpret a fresh attributed case detail without imposing the first community’s practices or confusing a later reconstruction/current institution with original period evidence.

Include distinct First Nation, Métis and Inuit examples and more than one settler community, with documented men’s, women’s and children’s contributions. Ask for a supported similarity and difference between two cases, then offer a new attributed detail: does it fit that community and period, or are they assuming everyone lived the same way?

topics.name: Economic sectors and activities
topics.description: In an explicitly stated four-sector economic model, distinguish natural-resource production or extraction, material processing or manufacturing, general services, and information or knowledge work. Name the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors, classify described industry activities by their main purpose, and recognize mixed activities without treating this convention as a universal legal business classification.

evidence: Explain the four sector names under the stated model and connect each with an accurately described example industry.

Distinguish resource production/extraction from processing/manufacturing, and general services from information/knowledge work under this four-sector convention; justify the distinction using the actual activity rather than its location, tools or prestige.

Classify unfamiliar but clearly described activities and recognize different sector activities within one organization, without assuming that every economic classification system separates services in the same way.

topics.name: Canada’s provinces, territories and capitals
topics.description: Know Canada’s ten provinces and three territories, locate them broadly on a political map and pair each with its provincial or territorial capital. Distinguish these capitals from Canada’s national capital, Ottawa, and recognize the same places in a changed map style rather than rely on one colour scheme.
