evidence: Name and broadly locate the ten provinces and three territories, distinguishing the two groups, without copying a complete visible answer list.

Why are Ottawa and Toronto different kinds of capital? Try a differently styled map too. Correct oral English or French names and broad pointing count; this is not a spelling or surveying test.

topics.name: Early First Nations and Inuit community life
topics.originalName: Early First Nations and Inuit community life
topics.description: Know a bounded repertoire of pre-1500 First Nation and Inuit community cases in what is now Canada. Identify each studied community and approximate period, describe supported food, shelter and material technologies, and explain particular connections to its local land, water and seasonal setting. Keep distinct communities and periods separate, and distinguish excavated remains, attributed interpretations and modern reconstructions.

topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, identify and broadly place one specific First Nation village and one early Inuit community in their different regions and approximate pre-1500 periods, rather than naming only broad present-day peoples.

Describe documented food, housing and material technologies in both studied cases, including a supported example of how local resources or seasonal conditions affected meeting needs. Use actual learned case facts rather than treating a generic Arctic or farming image as sufficient.

Use the learned knowledge to compare a supported similarity and difference, then respond to a changed-view or fresh attributed case detail without transferring another community’s practices or treating a modern reconstruction as an original period image.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After learning about a mid-15th-century St Lawrence village and a 14th-century Inuit winter village, can {{name}} identify each place and period, describe its food, homes and tools, and explain one supported link to its setting? Compare the cases, then show a new labelled view or detail: can they connect it to the right case without assuming all communities lived alike?

topics.name: Leadership in early First Nation and Inuit communities
topics.originalName: Leadership in early First Nation and Inuit communities
topics.description: Know a bounded, source-attributed repertoire of early community organisation: the Haudenosaunee founding-peace account and council/Clan Mother relationships, and a qualified reconstruction of leadership, crews and resource sharing in a Classic Thule Inuit whaling community. Explain the different roles and cooperation relationships without turning a traditional account or archaeological model into a universal political system.
topics.originalDescription: Know a bounded, source-attributed repertoire of early community organisation: the Haudenosaunee founding-peace account and council/Clan Mother relationships, and a qualified reconstruction of leadership, crews and resource sharing in a Classic Thule Inuit whaling community. topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, identify the Haudenosaunee founding-peace account and explain the relationship between distinct Nations, chiefs, Clan Mothers and shared council decisions. Attribute the account and distinguish its historical peace aim from a modern municipal council or one all-powerful ruler.

Describe the studied Classic Thule community reconstruction: organising cooperative harvesting involved leaders, crews and household/resource relationships. Explain the supported link between coordination, resource access and social roles/status, labelling the archaeological/analogy-based interpretation rather than claiming an observed constitution for every Inuit community.

Compare the two learned arrangements with a supported similarity and difference. Given a fresh attributed community account, use its own role/decision information instead of assuming the first case’s institutions or a fixed system based on ethnicity or region.
topics.assessmentPrompt: After learning the Haudenosaunee founding account and the studied early Inuit community reconstruction, can {{name}} explain who worked together, how roles differed and what cooperation helped achieve? Compare the cases, then offer a new attributed account: what can they conclude, and what remains uncertain?

topics.name: Continents on maps and globes
topics.description: Name and locate Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America using the stated seven-continent map model. Distinguish continents from countries and oceans, and recognize that geographical models and labels can differ; state the model being used rather than assume every map groups land in exactly the same way.

Distinguish continents from countries and oceans, and recognize that geographical models and labels can differ; state the model being used rather than assume every map groups land in exactly the same way.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Name and locate the seven continents in the stated model on a world map and globe without simply copying labels.
Distinguish a country, continent and ocean in familiar examples; recognize that Australia can name both a country and a continent in this model.
Locate the same continents on a differently centred map or turned globe and explain a different grouping/label convention when it is explicitly supplied.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Using the seven-continent model, can {{name}} name and locate Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America and South America on a map and globe, distinguish a country and an ocean from a continent, and still find the same continents on another view? If another map groups or labels land differently, can they say which model they are using rather than call every difference an error?

topics.name: Equator and Northern and Southern Hemispheres
topics.originalName: Equator and Northern and Southern Hemispheres
topics.description: Identify the Equator as an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the geographic poles, dividing Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Locate points or regions relative to it on maps and globes, using the geographic reference rather than the current top of a page or model.
topics.originalDescription: Identify the Equator as an imaginary circle around Earth halfway between the geographic poles, dividing Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Locate points or regions relative to it on maps and globes, using the geographic reference rather than the current top of a page or model.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Locate the Equator on a globe or world map and explain that it is an imaginary reference, not a physical wall or country border.
Identify the Northern Hemisphere on the North Pole side of the Equator and the Southern Hemisphere on the South Pole side.
Classify supplied points/regions as north, south or crossing the Equator, recognizing that a region may extend into both halves.
Transfer the reference to a turned globe or differently oriented/centred map without redefining north as whichever side is physically up.
topics.assessmentPrompt: On a globe and another world map, can {{name}} find the Equator, identify the Northern and Southern Hemispheres, and place some marked locations in the correct half? Can they explain a region that crosses the Equator and keep the same geographical references when the model or page is turned?

topics.name: Cardinal directions on maps
topics.description: Use a map’s stated north reference to identify north, south, east and west; describe where one labelled place lies relative to another and locate a selected place from a cardinal-direction statement. Retain the map reference when the whole map is turned, rather than treating physical page-up as north.
topics.originalDescription: Use a map’s stated north reference to identify north, south, east and west; describe where one labelled place lies relative to another and locate a selected place from a cardinal-direction statement. Retain the map reference when the whole map is turned, rather than treating physical page-up as north.
topics.subject: geografia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify north, south, east and west from a map’s north arrow or four-point compass rose.
Describe the cardinal direction from one selected labelled place to another, give the reverse relationship, and locate a place from a direction statement.
Use the same reference correctly on a new or turned map, with its arrow and places turned together; explain why page-up need not be north.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give {{name}} a simple labelled map with a north arrow and places lying directly north, south, east or west of one another. Can they name the four directions, tell you where one place is from another and give the reverse direction? Ask them to find a place from your direction clue, then turn the whole map, including its arrow, and try a new pair: do they still use the map reference instead of calling page-up north?

topics.name: Rights and civic responsibilities in Canada
topics.originalName: Rights and civic responsibilities in Canada
topics.description: Know selected rights and freedoms in Canada-equal protection under law, freedom of religion and expression, and eligible citizens’ federal voting rights-and explain related responsibilities to respect others’ rights, obey laws and contribute to community life. Distinguish general protections from citizenship/age-qualified voting, and legal duties from voluntary civic contributions.
topics.originalDescription: Know selected rights and freedoms in Canada-equal protection under law, freedom of religion and expression, and eligible citizens’ federal voting rights-and explain related responsibilities to respect others’ rights, obey laws and contribute to community life. Distinguish general protections from citizenship/age-qualified voting, and legal duties from voluntary civic contributions.
topics.subject: desenvolvimento-pessoal-social
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, explain equal protection under law and freedom of religion and expression in simple Canadian public-life cases. Recognise that general protections are not reserved only for citizens or Canadian-born people, and that rights are not unlimited permission to harm others.

Distinguish general protections from the basic federal elector qualifications of Canadian citizenship and being at least 18 on polling day. Recognise that actual voting also has procedures, and that a primary-age child can have rights and participate in community life without being qualified to cast a federal vote.

Explain responsibilities to obey laws and respect others’ rights, and describe a voluntary way to contribute to civic/community life. Do not make rights conditional on volunteering or agreeing with a political opinion; distinguish a government-related Charter question from every private disagreement.
topics.assessmentPrompt: A newcomer, a child and an adult citizen discuss a public decision in Canada. Can {{name}} explain their protections for equal treatment under law, religion and expression, who has the basic qualifications for a federal vote, and how they can act responsibly? Would someone have to volunteer to keep those rights?

Can {{name}} explain their protections for equal treatment under law, religion and expression, who has the basic qualifications for a federal vote, and how they can act responsibly? Would someone have to volunteer to keep those rights?

topics.name: Government duty to consult Indigenous peoples in Canada
topics.originalName: Government duty to consult Indigenous peoples in Canada
topics.description: Explain the federal/provincial Crown’s constitutional duty to meaningfully consult affected Indigenous rights-holding groups when contemplated government action may adversely affect potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights it knows or could reasonably know about, and to accommodate where appropriate. Use supplied cases to recognise when the duty may apply, distinguishing it from ordinary public opinion gathering without deciding a real legal claim.
topics.originalDescription: Explain the federal/provincial Crown’s constitutional duty to meaningfully consult affected Indigenous rights-holding groups when contemplated government action may adversely affect potential or established Aboriginal or treaty rights it knows or could reasonably know about, and to accommodate where appropriate. Use supplied cases to recognise when the duty may apply, distinguishing it from ordinary public opinion gathering without deciding a real legal claim.
topics.subject: desenvolvimento-pessoal-social
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Explain that the duty concerns the federal/provincial government and Indigenous rights-holding groups, including First Nations, Métis and Inuit where the relevant rights/impact conditions exist. It is a legal obligation relating to rights, not merely asking all nearby residents for an optional opinion.

Given plausible original scenarios with government action, credible potential or established rights the government knows or could reasonably know about, and a supported possible adverse impact explicitly supplied, explain why the duty may apply. For an incomplete case identify missing facts; ethnicity, proximity, a municipal border or the nearest reserve alone does not decide it.

Explain timely two-way information/listening and responsive consideration of concerns before the decision, with appropriate accommodation such as changing a proposed design to avoid or reduce harm. Do not treat one meeting as automatically adequate, consultation as automatic project approval or an unconditional universal veto, or delegated developer paperwork as removing the Crown’s ultimate responsibility.
topics.assessmentPrompt: A government is considering a fictional project and knows it could affect an Indigenous community’s stated harvesting rights. Can {{name}} explain why it may have a duty to consult and what meaningful consultation and possible accommodation are for? Change the case: if the rights or possible impact facts are missing, what would they need to know rather than just choosing the nearest reserve?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: A government is considering a fictional project and knows it could affect an Indigenous community’s stated harvesting rights. Can {{name}} explain why it may have a duty to consult and what meaningful consultation and possible accommodation are for? Change the case: if the rights or possible impact facts are missing, what would they need to know rather than just choosing the nearest reserve?

topics.name: Government responsibilities in Canada
topics.description: Explain the respective responsibilities of federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments in Canada, and distinguish these from the structures and roles of studied First Nation, Métis and Inuit governing or representative bodies and a publicly funded school board. Use concrete service and issue examples to show where responsibilities differ and where named bodies work together. Distinguish national representation, regional self-government, local government, departmental implementation and advisory roles rather than assign identical authority to every council or organisation. A geographic location or service name alone does not establish jurisdiction; Indigenous arrangements vary, and provincial and territorial authority have different constitutional origins.
topics.originalDescription: Explain the respective responsibilities of federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments in Canada, and distinguish these from the structures and roles of studied First Nation, Métis and Inuit governing or representative bodies and a publicly funded school board. Use concrete service and issue examples to show where responsibilities differ and where named bodies work together. Distinguish national representation, regional self-government, local government, departmental implementation and advisory roles rather than assign identical authority to every council or organisation. A geographic location or service name alone does not establish jurisdiction; Indigenous arrangements vary, and provincial and territorial authority have different constitutional origins.
topics.subject: desenvolvimento-pessoal-social
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify supported Canadian examples of federal national responsibilities, provincial and territorial responsibilities, and municipal services. Explain that municipalities exercise powers assigned within provincial or territorial arrangements, while territories are not simply provinces with a different name. A complete constitutional inventory is not required.

Describe studied current First Nation, Métis and Inuit governing or representative arrangements: identify their relevant local, regional or national structure, whom they represent and a supported function. Distinguish governing decisions from representation or advice, and do not assign identical powers to every Indigenous institution. Describe how a studied publicly funded school board operates schools within provincial education responsibility, distinguishing provincial curriculum/funding, board operation and school-council advice.

Explain distinct contributions of named bodies in a studied shared-service or social issue and a studied environmental issue, rather than only list government names. Use actual source-backed examples and retain their dates and limits.

Apply this knowledge to changed Canadian service/issue cases: identify a supported responsible body or shared role, explain the reason, and state what authority information is missing when the supplied facts do not establish it.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Who handles national defence, sets Ontario’s school curriculum, operates a local publicly funded school, or provides a municipal service? Can {{name}} explain the structures and supported roles of studied First Nation, Métis and Inuit governing or representative bodies, distinguishing a national representative voice from a regional self-government? Then show how named bodies share an education or environmental responsibility. Try a changed issue: what do they know, and what would they need to check?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Who handles national defence, sets Ontario’s school curriculum, operates a local publicly funded school, or provides a municipal service? Can {{name}} explain the structures and supported roles of studied First Nation, Métis and Inuit governing or representative bodies, distinguishing a national representative voice from a regional self-government? Then show how named bodies share an education or environmental responsibility. Try a changed issue: what do they know, and what would they need to check?

topics.name: Reading and recording staff notation
topics.description: Read and record short melodies in standard staff notation. Use the clef and staff positions, including nearby ledger lines, to identify pitches; note and rest values, bars and time signatures to organise duration; key signatures and accidentals to determine altered notes; and common tempo, dynamics, articulation and repeat signs to guide a sounded performance. Compare the score and audible result, repair a mismatch, and record a melody so another performer can recover it. Translate between a devised representation and staff notation while preserving the represented musical relationships.
topics.originalDescription: Read and record short melodies in standard staff notation. Use the clef and staff positions, including nearby ledger lines, to identify pitches; note and rest values, bars and time signatures to organise duration; key signatures and accidentals to determine altered notes; and common tempo, dynamics, articulation and repeat signs to guide a sounded performance. Compare the score and audible result, repair a mismatch, and record a melody so another performer can recover it. Translate between a devised representation and staff notation while preserving the represented musical relationships.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Perform a short previously unheard staff-notated melody, using its clef, pitch positions, key or accidental information, durations, rests and metre rather than copying a sounded model.
Record a short melody in staff notation so another performer can recover its pitch and rhythmic relationships, and use the indicated expressive or repeat signs where present.
Find and repair a meaningful mismatch in pitch, duration, rest, altered note or interpretation of a musical marking, rather than merely name the symbols.
Apply the same standard conventions to a changed melody and translate a short devised representation to or from a staff score, preserving the intended musical relationships.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} turn a short staff score into a sounded melody using its pitch, rhythm and musical markings, then record a melody another person can recover? Can they identify and fix a mismatch and use the same conventions on a different melody?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} turn a short staff score into a sounded melody using its pitch, rhythm and musical markings, then record a melody another person can recover? Can they identify and fix a mismatch and use the same conventions on a different melody?

topics.name: Mixing and adjusting paint colours
topics.description: Choose suitable safe paints and make an actual mixture for a chosen colour intention. Compare a sample with the intended result, decide on and make a purposeful adjustment, and check what changed. Use the observed mixing relationships to work towards a different target or to adjust to another suitable paint material. Success concerns deliberate mixing, comparison and adjustment, not a perfect colour match, one fixed recipe, technical colour names or choosing an already matched paint pot.
topics.originalDescription: Choose suitable safe paints and make an actual mixture for a chosen colour intention. Compare a sample with the intended result, decide on and make a purposeful adjustment, and check what changed. Use the observed mixing relationships to work towards a different target or to adjust to another suitable paint material. Success concerns deliberate mixing, comparison and adjustment, not a perfect colour match, one fixed recipe, technical colour names or choosing an already matched paint pot.
topics.subject: arte
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Choose paints for an intended mixture, test an actual sample and compare the result with a target or stated intended change.
Make a reasoned material adjustment to the mixture, show the before/after samples and judge whether it moved towards the intention rather than accept every random result.
Use what was observed to mix towards a different target or to test and adjust with a different safe paint set or medium; recognise that materials can behave differently.
topics.assessmentPrompt: With suitable paints and a target swatch or a colour change they choose, can {{name}} make and compare a mixture, deliberately adjust it and show what changed? Can they use what they noticed for another target or paint material, rather than only copy one recipe? An exact match and technical colour names are not required.
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: With suitable paints and a target swatch or a colour change they choose, can {{name}} make and compare a mixture, deliberately adjust it and show what changed? Can they use what they noticed for another target or paint material, rather than only copy one recipe? An exact match and technical colour names are not required.

topics.name: Institutions and roles in New France
topics.originalName: Institutions and roles in New France
topics.description: Describe a bounded repertoire of French colonial institutions in the St. Lawrence colony, chiefly during the royal regime from 1663 to 1713: the king and appointed governor and intendant, Catholic religious and education/care institutions, and the seigneurial landholding relationship. Explain supported roles, overlapping responsibilities and why they mattered to settlers. Keep the period, place and colonial perspective distinct from modern Canadian institutions, medieval serfdom and Indigenous governance or land rights.
topics.originalDescription: Describe a bounded repertoire of French colonial institutions in the St. Lawrence colony, chiefly during the royal regime from 1663 to 1713: the king and appointed governor and intendant, Catholic religious and education/care institutions, and the seigneurial landholding relationship. Explain supported roles, overlapping responsibilities and why they mattered to settlers. Keep the period, place and colonial perspective distinct from modern Canadian institutions, medieval serfdom and Indigenous governance or land rights.
topics.subject: historia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Place the learned institutional example in New France and its late-seventeenth/early-eighteenth-century setting. Explain the relationship between the French crown and appointed colonial officials, including the governor’s defence/diplomatic role and the intendant’s justice, administration and finance work; recognise that they also cooperated and had overlapping responsibilities.

Describe actual learned Catholic institutional roles, including religion and specific school/care examples. Identify a supported relationship such as the Ursulines’ education of girls or the Augustinians’ hospital work without assuming all people shared one belief, attended the same institution or had equal access.

Explain the studied seigneur/habitant landholding and responsibility relationship, using supported land, rent/labour or mill examples and why these mattered to settlers. Distinguish it from the colony’s governing offices rather than transplant a medieval king-knight-serf pyramid.

Use this knowledge to interpret a fresh attributed account of a settler-era administration, land or community-service situation, identifying a supported institution/role and explaining what remains uncertain. A colonial land grant or map does not by itself establish that Indigenous land was empty or that all Indigenous rights ended.

Give a new short account from the same period: which institution might be involved, why would it matter to settlers, and what can they not conclude from the account?

topics.name: Early colonial relationships and Métis emergence in Canada
topics.originalName: Early colonial relationships and Métis emergence in Canada
topics.description: Know a bounded repertoire of early Indigenous-European trade, settlement and alliance relationships in northeastern North America, and explain the longer-term emergence of distinct Métis communities from fur-trade relationships. Keep the studied Great Lakes-St. Lawrence, Mi’kmaq/Port-Royal and Qikiqtani Inuit encounters before 1713, including 1701 Montréal peace, distinct from the later collective ethnogenesis documented in the Great Lakes and Mattawa/Nipissing regions. Explain specific aims, exchanges, benefits, harms and changes without equating mixed ancestry alone with Métis identity.
topics.originalDescription: Know a bounded repertoire of early Indigenous-European trade, settlement and alliance relationships in northeastern North America, and explain the longer-term emergence of distinct Métis communities from fur-trade relationships. Keep the studied Great Lakes-St. Lawrence, Mi’kmaq/Port-Royal and Qikiqtani Inuit encounters before 1713, including 1701 Montréal peace, distinct from the later collective ethnogenesis documented in the Great Lakes and Mattawa/Nipissing regions. topics.subject: historia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: After study, identify the learned Great Lakes-St. Lawrence, Acadian and Qikiqtani Inuit cases and their approximate periods, rather than call all Indigenous peoples one group or substitute Australian colonial history.

Explain supported European commercial, route-seeking, settlement and religious aims alongside specific Indigenous trade, knowledge and diplomatic interests. Identify actual exchanges and why different parties could benefit, without presenting the relationships as equal or harmless.

Describe significant supported harms and changed relationships, including disease, captivity/conflict and negotiated peace, keeping actual actors and chronology distinct. Distinguish a hostile suspicion or later interpretation from established evidence and acknowledge continuing Indigenous peoples.

Explain how fur-trade dependence on First Nations knowledge, family relationships and kinship could contribute to later community formation. Distinguish these earlier causal conditions from collective Métis identity and culture: the studied sources place Great Lakes emergence in the late eighteenth/early nineteenth centuries and Mattawa/Nipissing emergence in the early nineteenth century. Métis are a distinct people, not everyone with mixed ancestry or a pre-1713 Mattawa community.

Use the retained knowledge in a fresh attributed account of a changed trade, settlement or alliance situation: explain a supported relationship or consequence and a fact the account cannot establish, rather than copy a generic contact story.

How did fur-trade knowledge and family relationships contribute to later distinct Métis communities in the Great Lakes and Mattawa regions, and why is that not the same as saying everyone with mixed ancestry was Métis before 1713? Try a changed short account: what is supported and what remains uncertain?

topics.name: Drawing one-point perspective
topics.description: Construct and interpret a simple one-point perspective drawing of a built space or box-like form viewed with a front plane facing the viewer. Choose a horizon and one vanishing point, draw depth directions towards that point while retaining the appropriate horizontal and vertical directions, and check the intended depth and relative size relationships. Repair an inconsistent depth line and transfer the construction to another simple arrangement or viewpoint. This is a converging representation, distinct from parallel isometric or oblique projection; exact physical scale, photorealism and two-point perspective are not required.

evidence: Choose a horizon and a vanishing point and construct an own simple room, pathway or box-like arrangement, showing which depth directions converge and which front-plane directions remain horizontal or vertical.

Construct another simple view after changing the position of the horizon, vanishing point or objects, preserving coherent convergence and visible surfaces without treating the drawing as a true-scale plan.

topics.name: Estimating quantities in visible collections
topics.description: Estimate approximately how many objects are in a visible, countable collection before enumerating every item. Use an available known quantity, visual grouping or another meaningful comparison to support the estimate, then count to check and reconcile the approximation with the actual quantity. Adapt the approach to a fresh unknown-total collection with a changed layout or material at an appropriate supplied task scale. This is approximate quantity judgement, distinct from exact one-to-one counting, instant recognition of a very small set, place-value representation or rounding an already written calculation.

evidence: Commit to an approximate quantity before exact item-by-item counting, indicating a relevant known group, visual grouping or comparison that supports the estimate; an unexplained arbitrary number or count-first answer is insufficient.

Count the actual collection accurately to check, compare the initial estimate with the result and explain what the comparison suggests about the estimate or chosen reference. An estimate may happen to be exact.

Use a fresh, not-yet-counted collection with a changed layout or material and adapt the reference/comparison rather than repeat a previous guess. Rearranging a known counted set preserves its exact total and is a separate cardinality contrast, not a new estimation trial.

topics.name: Locating places with latitude and longitude
topics.originalName: Locating places with latitude and longitude
topics.description: Use a labelled latitude/longitude graticule on a map or globe to locate and describe positions from the Equator and a stated zero-longitude reference. Interpret north/south and east/west degree values together and keep the same geographic position across changed views or representations. Read the stated coordinate labels, order and resolution rather than impose a Cartesian x-first rule or treat grid spacing as ground distance.
topics.originalDescription: Use a labelled latitude/longitude graticule on a map or globe to locate and describe positions from the Equator and a stated zero-longitude reference. evidence: Identify latitude as north/south of the Equator and longitude as east/west of the stated zero meridian, with the correct degree values and directional labels. Distinguish a line’s direction on the model from the direction its value measures.

Locate a supplied latitude/longitude position at the appropriate intersection and read both named coordinates of marked positions, including opposite-hemisphere contrasts and a zero-reference point, using the provided resolution.

Use supplied coordinates for a named place on a suitable map/globe and explain the approximation/precision given. A place label, guessed continent or one coordinate alone is not a complete geographic location.

Transfer to a new, turned or differently centred labelled representation, retaining the geographic references and stated field convention; do not infer equal physical distances from equal-looking flat-grid intervals.

Contrast north with south and east with west, then try a changed view: do they retain the geographic references and the supplied precision rather than swap the fields or use page-up?

topics.name: Jewish Canadian history, exclusion and community contributions
topics.originalName: Jewish Canadian history, exclusion and community contributions
topics.description: Know a bounded Jewish Canadian historical repertoire linking political and social exclusion with community action and contributions: Hart’s Lower Canada case, Toronto Mount Sinai’s founding, Canada’s St. Louis refugee refusal and Holocaust consequences, and the post-war international human-rights movement’s influence on Canadian protection. Explain particular actors, places, periods and changes without reducing Jewish life to victimhood, treating contributions as a condition for rights, or assuming legislation ended antisemitism.
topics.originalDescription: Know a bounded Jewish Canadian historical repertoire linking political and social exclusion with community action and contributions: Hart’s Lower Canada case, Toronto Mount Sinai’s founding, Canada’s St. Louis refugee refusal and Holocaust consequences, and the post-war international human-rights movement’s influence on Canadian protection. Explain particular actors, places, periods and changes without reducing Jewish life to victimhood, treating contributions as a condition for rights, or assuming legislation ended antisemitism.
topics.subject: historia
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify the studied Jewish Canadian cases and put their principal developments in the correct places and historical sequence, distinguishing Lower Canada from Ontario and wartime Europe from Canada.

Explain how antisemitic or religious exclusion affected political participation, professional/care opportunities and refuge in the selected cases, distinguishing what Canada did from Nazi crimes and avoiding an all-people or all-passengers generalisation.

Explain the particular community actions and contributions in the Hart family and Toronto hospital cases, including the hospital’s care for people beyond its founding community; rights do not have to be earned through achievement.

Explain how the experience of the Second World War and Holocaust contributed to international human-rights efforts and influenced later Canadian protections, distinguishing the 1948 declaration from Canadian statutes/constitutional protection and recognising continuing discrimination.

Use the learned repertoire to assess a new short historical claim or supplied comparison: identify supported connection, date/place/scope error or missing evidence rather than guess a new person’s experience or substitute a generic statement to be kind.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what changed in the Hart and Toronto hospital cases, how Canada responded to the St. Louis refugees, and how post-war human-rights efforts influenced later Canadian protection? Try a new claim: do they keep the dates, places and limits clear without saying rights were earned or discrimination disappeared?
topics.originalAssessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain what changed in the Hart and Toronto hospital cases, how Canada responded to the St. Louis refugees, and how post-war human-rights efforts influenced later Canadian protection? Try a new claim: do they keep the dates, places and limits clear without saying rights were earned or discrimination disappeared?

topics.name: Loads and internal forces in structures
topics.originalName: Loads and internal forces in structures
topics.description: Distinguish external loading from forces transmitted within a simple structure or member. Identify internal tension and compression, explain their stretching or squeezing effects, and use a specified supported-beam case to explain why bending can combine both even when the structure remains still.
topics.originalDescription: Distinguish external loading from forces transmitted within a simple structure or member. Identify internal tension and compression, explain their stretching or squeezing effects, and use a specified supported-beam case to explain why bending can combine both even when the structure remains still.
topics.subject: ciencias
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Name the chosen structure/member and distinguish a supplied external load or support interaction from internal tension/compression within it.
Explain tension in a hanging tie/cable and compression in a supporting column, relating each to a tendency to stretch or shorten and possible deformation rather than assuming immediate failure.

For a simply supported horizontal beam sagging under a downward central load, identify upper compression and lower tension; explain that balanced external forces do not mean an absence of internal forces.

Transfer the load-to-internal-effect reasoning to a changed orientation or support case, using supplied facts and stating when more information is needed rather than assuming top always means compression.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain how a hanging cord and a supporting column carry a load differently, then show where a beam supported at both ends squeezes and stretches as a weight bends its middle down-even while the whole structure stays still?

topics.name: Food allergies and sensitivities
topics.description: Recognise that some foods can cause harmful reactions in particular people even when those foods are safe for others. Identify several common food-allergy triggers and possible reactions, distinguish an allergy from a non-allergic food intolerance using familiar examples, and explain why a possible reaction calls for adult help rather than tasting a food to test it or diagnosing the cause from symptoms alone.
topics.originalDescription: Recognise that some foods can cause harmful reactions in particular people even when those foods are safe for others. Identify several common food-allergy triggers and possible reactions, distinguish an allergy from a non-allergic food intolerance using familiar examples, and explain why a possible reaction calls for adult help rather than tasting a food to test it or diagnosing the cause from symptoms alone.
topics.subject: habilidades-para-vida
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Identify several common food-allergy triggers across different kinds of food, such as milk, egg, peanuts or tree nuts, and fish; explain that this is not a complete list and that a food can be nutritious for many people yet unsafe for someone with a particular allergy.

Use fictional cases to explain that a food allergy can involve the immune system and cause skin, breathing or digestive reactions, sometimes seriously; contrast a known lactose-intolerance case involving difficulty digesting milk sugar, while recognising that the same food can be associated with different conditions and that symptoms alone do not establish a diagnosis.

For a changed fictional case involving a possible food reaction, identify prompt adult help and the supplied individual care or emergency procedure, without proposing a food challenge, medicine dose or independent diagnosis.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Using picture cases, can {{name}} name several foods that can trigger an allergy, explain why a milk allergy and lactose intolerance are different even though both can involve milk, and say what to do if someone may be reacting to food?

topics.name: Prescription and non-prescription medicines
topics.description: Distinguish a medicine that requires a prescription for a particular person from one available without a prescription under the applicable local system. Explain that both can have benefits and risks, and use the distinction to explain adult-supported safety rules: use only an appropriate medicine under the supplied professional or label instructions, do not share another person’s prescription, and obtain help rather than guess when the person, instructions or medicine are uncertain. This is safety knowledge, not diagnosis, choosing a treatment or administering a dose.
topics.originalDescription: Distinguish a medicine that requires a prescription for a particular person from one available without a prescription under the applicable local system. Explain that both can have benefits and risks, and use the distinction to explain adult-supported safety rules: use only an appropriate medicine under the supplied professional or label instructions, do not share another person’s prescription, and obtain help rather than guess when the person, instructions or medicine are uncertain. This is safety knowledge, not diagnosis, choosing a treatment or administering a dose.
topics.subject: habilidades-para-vida
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.
evidence: Using familiar examples with their local status supplied, explain why an antibiotic prescribed for a named person is a prescription medicine while a declared over-the-counter pain-relief product does not require a prescription; do not infer status or safety from colour, taste, advertising or the word natural.

Explain why neither prescription nor over-the-counter status makes a medicine safe for any person in any amount: the responsible adult checks the intended person, purpose, directions and relevant professional advice, and keeps medicine securely stored rather than sharing or leaving it accessible.

Use a changed fictional case involving a friend’s prescription, unclear directions or an unfamiliar product to explain stopping and obtaining responsible adult/pharmacist help, without choosing a treatment, calculating a dose, altering a medicine or testing it by tasting.
topics.assessmentPrompt: Using two practice cards-an antibiotic prescribed for Sam and a medicine declared available without a prescription-can {{name}} explain the difference and why both still need appropriate adult guidance? What should happen if a friend offers Sam’s medicine or the instructions are unclear?

topics.name: How flight forces work
topics.description: Explain a qualitative model of aerodynamic flight: interaction with air can create drag opposing the flyer's motion relative to surrounding air and lift perpendicular to that relative motion; gravity supplies weight and a propulsion system can supply thrust. Identify the origins and directions of these forces, use their resultant to explain steady or changing flight, and explain how changing airflow, a surface, propulsion or carried mass can alter the force account. Distinguish aerodynamic lift from buoyancy; do not require aerodynamic equations, piloting procedures or a full fluid-mechanics theory.
topics.originalDescription: Explain a qualitative model of aerodynamic flight: interaction with air can create drag opposing the flyer's motion relative to surrounding air and lift perpendicular to that relative motion; gravity supplies weight and a propulsion system can supply thrust. Identify the origins and directions of these forces, use their resultant to explain steady or changing flight, and explain how changing airflow, a surface, propulsion or carried mass can alter the force account. Distinguish aerodynamic lift from buoyancy; do not require aerodynamic equations, piloting procedures or a full fluid-mechanics theory.
topics.subject: ciencias
topics.gradeNote: Faixa aproximada por idade da fonte; não equivale ao ano curricular brasileiro.

prerequisites.reason: The complete prior pushes/pulls claim supplies force strength and direction causing motion changes, which the qualitative flight account presupposes.
A familiar resistance account supports drag, but its full water/surface repertoire is not intrinsic to explaining the wing/air model.

evidence: Identify lift, drag, weight and thrust in a supplied aircraft case, explaining where each comes from and its direction: drag opposes the flyer's motion relative to surrounding air, lift is perpendicular to that motion, and weight points towards Earth. Explain that lift comes from interaction with moving air, is not merely buoyancy and cannot be inferred from a curved wing drawing or an equal-transit-time story alone.

Explain a straight, level constant-velocity case with balanced forces and an initial changed-force case that speeds up, slows or changes direction. Distinguish constant velocity from being stationary, and recognise that a constant-speed turn still changes velocity; use supplied arrows or an ordinary-language account without requiring a new drawing procedure.

Explain bounded ways to change the force account through propulsion setting, surface shape/orientation, relative airflow or carried mass. Name which forces are affected, allow interacting effects and reject the rule that increasing a wing angle always improves lift.

Transfer the model to a contrasting supplied flyer such as an unpowered descending glider or a time-averaged bird case. Explain why no engine does not mean no aerodynamic lift, why all four forces need not be nonzero, and why a straight-level diagram cannot simply be copied into every situation.
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a model plane flying straight at a steady speed and then changing speed or direction, can they explain what lift, weight, thrust and drag are doing, where the air forces come from, and why an engine is not the same thing as the force holding the wings up?

KS3 graphing (lines of best fit, gradients) extends KS2 ability to construct and interpret line graphs and scatter graphs
'Text Features & Presentation' supports 'How texts in subjects differ'
'How texts in subjects differ' builds on 'Non-Fiction Text Features'
Solving word problems within 10 requires ability to represent the operations with objects/drawings
Multiplicative relationships require 'multiplicative relationship', 'direct proportion', and 'rate' vocabulary
Understanding multiplicative relationships as ratios or fractions is reinforced by the double number line and proportion graph
Connecting ratios to linear functions links to understanding y = mx + c from algebra
Connecting ratios to fractions requires expressing quantities as fractions of each other
Understanding multiplicative relationships requires fluent ratio notation

Recognising particular letter forms supports sight-word reading; an automatic 20-30-word connected-text bank with unusual spelling/sound correspondences can be demonstrated without naming both cases of all 26 letters, reciting A-Z and naming alternative spellings.
Blending helps attempt unfamiliar words but sight words bypass phonics
Performance connects to understanding how dramatists communicate through staging choices
Developing a model of matter as particles too small to see is built on the particle diagram representation
Must observe state changes before explaining them with particle model
Must understand observable states of matter before modelling them with particles
Data representation formats (pictograms, tally charts) support organising data
Counting data in categories requires understanding cardinality
Organising and representing data requires data, tally, frequency, and category vocabulary
Organising data in categories builds on classifying and counting objects in categories
Rhyme awareness is essential for writing poetry
Recognising literary language supports writing poetry
Writing poetry draws on 'compose', 'pattern', and 'genre' vocabulary
Oral rehearsal supports composing poems aloud
Reciting poems supports writing poetry - understanding performance element
Using Egyptian artefacts as evidence applies the general skill of using objects as evidence
Tomb paintings depict gods - knowing the gods helps interpret the art
Using artefacts as evidence builds on knowing what archaeologists do
Using tomb paintings and artefacts as evidence requires 'artefact', 'tomb', 'archaeologist' vocabulary
Using tomb paintings, papyri, and artefacts as evidence draws on the non-fiction reading skills for understanding how documents and visual texts are organised
Sexual selection and game theory depends on animal intelligence and complex behaviour
Sexual selection and evolutionary game theory depends on understanding co-evolutionary dynamics and the Red Queen hypothesis
Must know diverse life cycles before comparing reproductive strategies
Must know plant pollination and seed formation before learning about sexual vs asexual plant reproduction
Relative pronouns (who, which, that) overlap with pronoun knowledge; pronoun cohesion supports understanding pronoun reference in relative clauses
Relative clauses extend subordination; learners must understand how subordinate clauses work before embedding relative clauses
Answering 'how many?' requires the cardinality principle
Counting objects to answer 'how many?' requires one-to-one correspondence
Comparing and grouping materials as solids, liquids, or gases requires the naming vocabulary for the three states
Comparing and grouping solids, liquids, and gases by properties is greatly aided by the particle diagram representation
Must classify states of matter before understanding changes between states
Must group materials by properties before classifying into three states of matter
Changing shapes of solids provides context for understanding solid properties
Scale factor problems are key Y6 modelling contexts
Y6 modelling extends Y5 real-world problem modelling
Volume formula application is key Y6 modelling context
Must understand what minibeasts are before learning to name specific ones
Navigating print and screen texts builds on concepts of print (directionality, page by page)
Knowing non-fiction features (contents, index) helps print navigation, but basic screen navigation does not require it
Comparing written numerals is the symbolic form of comparing quantities - conceptual comparison helps but isn't strictly required
Debating requires skills in constructing arguments with evidence from argument writing
Formal debate requires confident public speaking skills first
Prepared discussion builds on gaining/maintaining listener interest and evaluating viewpoints
Coming to discussions prepared extends active collaborative conversation skills
Must know common species before classifying them into Saurischia and Ornithischia
Must understand basic diet classification before advancing to anatomical classification
Explaining conduction and convection at the particle level requires knowing the particle model of matter
Conduction, convection and radiation are three of the pathways for energy transfer by heating - the stores/transfers framework provides the structure
Must know circulatory system before understanding how it transports nutrients
Describing nutrient and water transport within animals requires organ system vocabulary
Must know digestive system before understanding nutrient absorption into blood
Body-emotion connection builds on understanding emotional triggers
Solving word problems within 100 requires fluent computation within 100
writing an equation with a symbol for the unknown builds on its meaning
Word problems within 100 extend word problems within 20
Comparing angles to right and straight angles supports estimating in degrees
Estimating/comparing angles requires understanding the degree system
Bioaccumulation occurs through food chains and webs - the feeding relationships must be understood first
Columnar add/sub with 4 digits is prerequisite to >4 digits
Reading approximate values from graphs requires graph-plotting experience
Estimating from quadratic graphs requires understanding how curves behave
Ocean floor concept requires knowing the ocean is vast and deep
Ocean floor is the bottom of the deepest zone; zone knowledge enriches it
KS3 sequence generation extends KS2 linear number sequences
Position-to-term rules require substituting the position number into a formula
Must understand sentences before joining them
Savanna animals contrasts with farm/pet animals from earlier
Savanna animals builds on knowing animals live in diverse environments
Sun-driven weather benefits from weather vs climate distinction
Sun as weather engine requires understanding the water cycle it drives
Sun drives weather builds on curriculum sunlight warms Earth's surface
Sun-driven weather systems extend the basic wind-cause concept to global scale
Tenths extend fraction understanding from halves, thirds, quarters
Skip counting supports counting in tenths
'Variables in programs' builds on 'Decisions and input in programs'
'Missing number problems (age 7+)' supports 'Variables in programs'
Confident spoken Standard English requires understanding spoken vs written language differences
Must understand plural -s before distinguishing possessive 's
Understanding apostrophe in contractions helps understand its use in possession
Understanding nouns supports identifying what can be possessive
Comparing test data from two designs is useful background, but interviewing a user and stating a need, measurable success criteria and constraints does not require first testing two existing designs
Translating real-world situations into algebra requires notation fluency
Modelling with algebra requires setting up and solving equations
Rock cycle benefits from knowing Earth's internal heat drives melting
The rock cycle connects the three rock types already learned
Rock cycle concept benefits from prior understanding of weathering and erosion
Social reflection benefits from feedback experience
Recognising patterns in how you interact with others is the Friendship domain-specific form of the foundational pattern-noticing habit
Reflecting on your role and behaviour in relationships builds on the foundational habit of considering the impact of your behaviour on others
Reflecting on social patterns builds on assertive communication skills
Knowing a range of polar animals enriches the detailed comparison
Detailed comparison builds on basic Arctic vs Antarctic distinction
Must distinguish objects from materials before naming specific materials
Literary vocabulary including mythological allusions builds on recognising literary language and sensory words; the step up is from identifying figurative language to interpreting allusions
Understanding literary vocabulary requires the ability to distinguish literal from figurative meaning
Temperature homeostasis links to enzyme activity in respiration and why stable temperature matters for cell function
'Similarities & Differences' supports 'Celebrations we share'
Reciting/presenting builds on Y1 oral description/expression
Articulating opinions supports presentation skills
Must spell root words before adding prefixes
Spelling with prefixes requires knowing 'prefix' and 'root word' as distinct, named concepts
Informative writing extends KS2 use of layout devices (headings, columns, bullets)
Writing well-structured informative/explanatory texts that examine a topic clearly requires the foundational ability to produce coherent, task/purpose-appropriate writing

Writing informative/explanatory texts with logical organisation and clear development of ideas across sections requires the ability to use cohesive devices and transitions to create coherence at whole-text level
Writing to explain requires understanding audience and purpose from KS2
Measuring mass with units requires first being able to compare masses directly
Word problems require understanding what products mean
Word problems require understanding what quotients mean
Every MAD calculation starts by finding the mean and ends by averaging the distances, so calculating and interpreting the mean is essential
Seeing spread as a feature of a distribution helps pupils interpret what a larger or smaller MAD says about the data
Understanding absolute value as a distance on the number line supports treating each deviation from the mean as a positive distance
Using MAD to compare spread builds on knowing that a single number (first the range) can summarise how much values vary, and on comparing two data sets by centre and spread
Must perform tests before learning to gather and record data
Skip counting in tens supports recognising decade numbers
Understanding decade numbers as 'some tens and 0 ones' requires the concept of a ten
Must know the sun is a star and planets orbit it before arguing about star brightness and distance
Enrichment knowledge of star brightness vs distance supports formal argument about apparent brightness
Must be able to group materials before conducting investigation to classify by properties
Romulus & Remus needs geographic context of Italy/Rome
Non-fiction structures build on Y1 informational text main topic
Understanding text features builds on Y1 book features
reading connected text aloud follows left-to-right, top-to-bottom, page-by-page print

A wider range of grapheme-phoneme correspondences supports reading more texts; accurate, meaningful emergent reading of a text matched to already taught correspondences does not require responding to the entire 40+ phoneme inventory first.
Need sight word bank for fluency
Must recognise common minibeasts before exploring where each type lives
ethics/citizenship vocabulary supports digital citizenship but is not required to be kind and safe online
Digital citizenship benefits from understanding bullying (cyberbullying)
Digital citizenship builds on basic safety awareness
being kind online starts from knowing that the people behind screens have their own feelings and thoughts
Y6 strategic tool use extends Y5 tool selection
Coordinate grids are a new tool for verification
Choosing long vs short division exemplifies Y6 strategic tool use
Identifying the repeating unit requires copying and continuing repeating patterns
Must understand erosion before comparing fast vs slow Earth events
Rock knowledge supports understanding geological events
Comparing capacity requires understanding capacity as a measurable attribute
Multiplication and division by powers of ten support metric conversions; non-base-ten time rates use their actual relationships.
Must understand how light works before designing a communication device using it
Must add/sub mixed numbers before solving word problems with them
Character/narrator analysis builds on Y1 story elements
Expressive reading supports deeper character analysis
KS3 photosynthesis provides the contrast needed to understand chemosynthesis as an alternative energy pathway
Photosynthesis requires knowing about chloroplasts, which are unique to plant cells
KS3 photosynthesis equation and process extends KS2 understanding that plants need light and water to grow
Must understand deforestation before discussing the complex future trade-offs
Climate connection is one of the competing priorities in the future debate
Must know conservation approaches before discussing balancing competing needs
Decimal notation for fractions is prerequisite to understanding % as parts per 100
Understanding the % symbol and 'per cent means parts per hundred' is the LANGUAGE node content
Age 6-7 strategic tool selection builds on age 5-6 familiarity with basic tools
Measuring length with units requires selecting appropriate measurement tools
Adding within 100 requires choosing number line vs hundred square strategically
Sentence crafting builds on clause knowledge
Sentence crafting uses relative clauses
Fraction-of-quantity skills support scaling by simple fractions
Multiplicative comparison supports scaling problems
Reading × and ÷ symbols parallels reading + and − symbols
Writing ÷ sentences requires understanding division
Writing × sentences requires understanding multiplication
Responsible design thinking extends to environmental considerations
Cross-domain: climate change awareness (Weather & Climate) enriches understanding of AI's environmental costs and benefits
Must understand training requires computation before grasping its environmental cost
Understanding alveoli and gas exchange requires knowing the cells-to-systems hierarchy
Detailed respiratory system builds on knowing we breathe air into lungs for oxygen
Following an algorithm builds on following step-by-step instructions
Describing pattern rules supports describing the number patterns an algorithm produces
Recognising number patterns supports describing what an algorithm produces
Understanding needs vs wants helps motivate saving decisions
Must understand what money is before learning to save it
Monitoring relates to active vs dormant classification
Monitoring benefits from plate tectonics context
Monitoring volcanoes requires understanding internal structure and eruption process
Compass constructions require confident drawing and measuring skills first
The reactivity series orders metals by their chemical reactivity - metal properties must be understood first
Displacement reactions are a key application of the reactivity series - reaction types must be understood first
Calculating probability using favourable/total outcomes requires understanding probability as a number on a 0-1 scale
The probability formula only applies to situations with equally likely outcomes - this concept must be secure first
Understanding subtraction as taking away requires knowing numbers represent quantities (cardinality)
Drawing shapes by attributes extends understanding defining vs non-defining attributes
Identifying pentagons, hexagons, quadrilaterals extends knowing 2-D shape properties
Understanding the general water cycle helps understand the rainforest-specific water cycle (Weather 7-9 -> Rainforests 7-9)
Understanding tropical climate (heat + rain) is prerequisite to understanding the water cycle within the forest
Knowing about rainforest plants helps understand transpiration from leaves
Atoms and molecules are the particles referred to in the particle model - builds directly on it
Looking for pairs that make 10 benefits from knowing number bonds to 10
Spotting a pair that makes 10 and adding it first means reordering addends, which relies on knowing that addition can be done in any order
US route: the associative property formalises grouping any two of the three addends first; soft because this node is US-only and England teaches the grouping within adding three one-digit numbers
Research and note-taking skills support the ability to gather and organise evidence from informational sources
Drawing evidence from informational texts requires the ability to identify main ideas across paragraphs
Explanations require place-value language and understanding
Must be able to use strategies before explaining why they work
'People shaping places' builds on 'Deforestation Causes & Scale'
'People shaping places' builds on 'Caring for Country and resources'
Must understand the medieval Church's power before grasping why Crusades were launched
Knight knowledge provides military context for the Crusades
Measuring length supports checking an invariance prediction; the conceptual prediction can also be discussed with a supplied comparison, so this is not a hard gate.
Liquid measurement supports a fair check of the prediction; the conceptual reasoning need not be gated on independent instrument reading.
Capacity and volume comparison language supports explaining the apparent-height trap but can be supplied orally in the task.
Ordering events supports the transmission story; dated timeline construction is not a hard prerequisite for explaining a supplied sequence.
Place-value understanding supports interpreting a placeholder example in the historical account; a supplied model can also provide that meaning.
Objects and drawings can externalise the relationships needed to pose a mathematical question; full prior mastery of solving a supplied model is not a hard gate.
Mathematical vocabulary can help express the question and its criterion, but pointing, drawings or a model allow formulation without a hard English grammar / question-word gate.
The complete prior pushes/pulls claim supplies force strength and direction causing motion changes, which the qualitative flight account presupposes.
A familiar resistance account supports drag, but its full water/surface repertoire is not intrinsic to explaining the wing/air model.
